name: Company rule in India
info: Company rule in India was the government of the British East India Company over much of the Indian subcontinent from the Battle of Plassey in 1757 until the Crown took over after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

facts.capital: Calcutta (Fort William), seat of the Governor-General from 1773
facts.founder: The East India Company; Robert Clive won Plassey, Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General
facts.predecessor: The Mughal Empire and its successor states, among them the Nawabs of Bengal
facts.successor: The British Raj, under the Government of India Act 1858

t: The Company's rule is variously dated from the Battle of Plassey in 1757, the grant of the diwani of Bengal and Bihar in 1765, or the appointment of Warren Hastings as Governor-General in 1773.
It expanded by outright annexation and by subsidiary alliances with Indian princes, whose territories made up two-thirds of India in the early 19th century.
In the Indian rebellion of 1857 almost the entire Bengal army revolted, and in 1858 the British government took over the direct administration of India.
dyk: In the Bengal famine of 1769–70, which the Company's uncertain revenue farming may have gravely worsened, between seven and ten million people, a quarter to a third of the presidency's population, may have died.
ev: Robert Clive's victory at the Battle of Plassey replaced the Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah with Mir Jafar
After the Battle of Buxar Shah Alam II appointed the Company diwan of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
The Regulating Act 1773 made Warren Hastings Governor-General of Fort William and placed the Company under parliamentary oversight
Lord Cornwallis promulgated the Permanent Settlement of land revenue in Bengal
The Anglo-Maratha wars ended, leaving no native power that threatened the Company
The Saint Helena Act ended the Company's China monopoly and made it an agent for the administration of British India
The Punjab was annexed after the Anglo-Sikh Wars, followed by Berar in 1854 and Oudh in 1856
The Indian rebellion of 1857 was followed by the Government of India Act 1858, which ended Company rule

sections.foundation:
The English East India Company was founded in 1600 as The Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies. It set up a factory at Masulipatnam in 1611, gained rights at Surat from the Mughal Emperor Jahangir in 1612, built a factory at Madras in 1640 and leased Bombay island in 1668; after the Anglo-Mughal War Aurangzeb let it settle at Calcutta. Its beginnings on the coast, among Portuguese, Dutch, French and Danish rivals, gave no sign of what was to come.

Robert Clive's victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 deposed the Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daulah in favour of Mir Jafar, and the Battle of Buxar in 1764 forced the emperor Shah Alam II to appoint the Company diwan, or revenue collector, of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765. By 1773 it was the de facto ruler of much of the Lower Gangetic Plain, and that year it abolished local rule in Bengal and made Calcutta its capital, with Warren Hastings as the first Governor-General. Historians date the beginning of Company rule to any of these three years.
sections.socioeconomy:
Land revenue was the government's primary function. The Company inherited a Mughal system in which zamindars collected rent from cultivators and paid revenue to the state, and its early tax farming may have gravely worsened the Bengal famine of 1769–70. In 1793 Lord Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement recognised rajas and taluqdars as zamindars and fixed the land tax in perpetuity, at a high level; peasants bore the brunt, forced labour spread, and up to one-third of zamindari lands were auctioned in two decades. In the south Thomas Munro's ryotwari system settled revenue directly with the peasants. In the 1850s Indian revenue agents were found using torture to meet the Company's demands.

Trade was transformed. Between 1780 and 1860 India changed from an exporter of fine cotton and silk paid for in bullion to an exporter of raw cotton, opium and indigo and a buyer of British manufactures. Opium grown under a government monopoly in the Ganges plain paid for Chinese tea and came to make up 40% of India's exports; historian Rolf Bauer says its cultivators were paid less than it cost to grow and the system depended on coercion. Indigo planters coerced peasants as well, until the Indigo rebellion of 1859–60.
sections.military:
On becoming Governor-General in 1772, Hastings rapidly expanded the Presidency's army, recruiting high-caste Rajputs and Brahmins of eastern Awadh and Bihar, the Purbiyas, who came to make up up to eighty per cent of the Bengal army. The Company respected their caste rules, with separate dining and no overseas service, and paid them well and reliably out of Bengal's land revenue. Red-coated sepoys under British officers aroused awe in their adversaries, and Indian rulers copied their red jackets.

The Anglo-Mysore wars (1766–1799) and the Anglo-Maratha wars (1772–1818) left the Company in control of much of India south of the Sutlej, and after the Marathas' defeat no native power threatened it. The Bengal army also served in the Third Anglo-Mysore War, in Java and in Ceylon. By the Vellore Mutiny of 1806 the three presidencies' armies numbered 154,500, one of the largest standing armies in the world. Irregular forces were added as territory grew, among them the Punjab Irregular Force of 1849. The Anglo-Sikh Wars brought the Punjab, and the First Opium War, fought to keep the opium trade with Qing China, gained five Chinese ports and Hong Kong under the Treaty of Nanjing.
sections.governance:
The Regulating Act 1773 let the Company act as a sovereign power on behalf of the Crown under parliamentary oversight, gave the Presidency of Fort William supremacy over Madras and Bombay, and named Warren Hastings Governor-General with four councillors. Pitt's India Act of 1784 created a Board of Control in London, and from then the British government had the final word on senior appointments. The attempted Impeachment of Warren Hastings, led by Edmund Burke from 1788, ended in acquittal in 1795. The Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's monopoly except for tea and the China trade, and the Saint Helena Act 1833 made it an agent of administration and the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.

The Company ruled annexed lands directly as British India and the rest through subsidiary alliances with the princely states, from Hyderabad in 1798 to Bahawalpur in 1833. Hastings set up district civil courts, diwani adalats, with Hindu pandits and Muslim qazis to interpret customary law, beside criminal courts and a Supreme Court at Fort William. Persian was abolished as the official language by 1837. A civil service of at most about 600 Britons, many trained at the East India Company College, ran taxes, customs and justice.
sections.impact:
Company rule laid the frame of the later British Raj. Its Supreme Courts and adalats survived until 1861, and its revenue settlements defined land ownership for a century. After 1813 Orientalist policy gave way to Anglicisation: the Asiatick Society of William Jones (1784), the Benares Sanskrit College (1791) and the College of Fort William (1800), which helped the Bengal Renaissance, were followed by Thomas Babington Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education of 1835 and the Education Dispatch of 1854. The universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras opened in 1857. The Company outlawed sati and thuggee, and the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856 gave remarrying widows some legal protection, though very few remarried.

It also built the first India-wide networks. A public post was set up in 1837 and postage stamps under the Indian Postal Act of 1854; W. B. O'Shaughnessy's telegraph trial of 1851 grew to 4,555 miles of lines by 1857. The first railway, from Bombay to Thane, opened in 1853 after Lord Dalhousie's Railway minute planned the trunk lines. The Ganges Canal, built under Sir Proby Cautley between 1842 and 1854, was in Ian Stone's words the largest canal ever attempted in the world.
sections.decline:
British unease over the Company grew from the start. By 1772 it needed government loans to stay afloat while its servants, the "Nabobs", came home rich, and each charter act took away more of its powers. After it lost its trading rights, land revenue became roughly half of government income, yet between 1814 and 1859 the government of India ran debts in 33 years, leaving little money for public works.

Dalhousie's annexations, the Punjab, Berar in 1854 and Oudh in 1856, unsettled the sepoys of the Bengal army, many of whom lost their perquisites as landed gentry in the Oudh courts and feared higher land revenue, while service in Burma and the loss of "foreign service" pay bred resentment. In the Indian rebellion of 1857 almost the entire Bengal army revolted, and rebels destroyed more than seven hundred miles of telegraph lines; the Bombay and Madras armies and the Hyderabad contingent stayed loyal, and the Punjab Irregular Force helped suppress the rising. Under the Government of India Act 1858 the India Office of the British government took over the direct administration of India in the new British Raj, and the army was reorganised.

summary: Company rule in India began when a London trading company, after Plassey and Buxar, took the revenues of Bengal and went on, by war, annexation and subsidiary alliances, to dominate the subcontinent. Regulated ever more closely by Parliament, it reshaped land, trade, law and education until the rebellion of 1857 led the Crown to take India over in 1858.

pointDescs.1757: Robert Clive's victory at Plassey replaced the Nawab of Bengal with the Company's ally Mir Jafar.
pointDescs.1765: After Buxar the Company was granted the diwani, the right to collect revenue, in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
pointDescs.1773: The Regulating Act made Warren Hastings Governor-General and Calcutta the capital of the Company's dominions.
pointDescs.1793: The Permanent Settlement fixed the land tax of Bengal in perpetuity.
pointDescs.1799: The Anglo-Mysore wars ended, and Mysore became a princely state under a subsidiary alliance.
pointDescs.1803: Delhi was annexed, two years after the North-Western Provinces.
pointDescs.1818: The end of the Anglo-Maratha wars left no native power able to threaten the Company; Rajputana entered alliance.
pointDescs.1833: The Saint Helena Act made the Company an agent for the administration of British India and created the Governor-General of India.
pointDescs.1849: The Punjab was annexed after the Anglo-Sikh Wars.
pointDescs.1856: The annexation of Oudh followed that of Berar in 1854, the height of the Company's dominion.
pointDescs.1857: Almost the entire Bengal army revolted in the Indian rebellion of 1857.
pointDescs.1858: The Government of India Act 1858 transferred the administration of India to the British government.
